questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
4{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4x{y}^{′}-16y=5x-2,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=\frac{A}{{x}^{2}}+B{x}^{2}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is  $5x-2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta ,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}\cdot 0+4x(\alpha )-16(\alpha x+\beta ) & =5x-2 \\ (4\alpha -16\alpha )x-16\beta  & =5x-2 \\ -12\alpha x-16\beta  & =5x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-12\alpha =5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ -16\beta =-2\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{5}{12},\,\,\beta =\frac{1}{8}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{5x}{12}+\frac{1}{8}.
$$

$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)=A+\frac{B}{t}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {t}^{3}+\beta {t}^{2},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are the constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=3\alpha {t}^{2}+2\beta t,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=6\alpha t+2\beta .
$$

 

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}(6\alpha t+2\beta )+2t(3\alpha {t}^{2}+2\beta t) & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2} \\ (6\alpha +6\alpha ){t}^{3}+(2\beta +4\beta ){t}^{2} & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2} \\ 12\alpha {t}^{3}+6\beta {t}^{2} & =12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12\alpha =12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{t}^{3}) \\ 6\beta =-24\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{t}^{2})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\,\,\beta =-4.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)={t}^{3}-4{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-4y=6x,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-4y=0.
$$

Let $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}-4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }-4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -4] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2$ and $\lambda =2.$ Thus, the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=\frac{{c}_{1}}{{x}^{2}}+{c}_{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is proportional to $6x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x
$$

where $\alpha $ is the constant that is to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(0)+x(\alpha )-4(\alpha x) & =6x \\ (\alpha -4\alpha )x & =6x \\ -3\alpha x & =6x\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get $\alpha =-2.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2x.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{{x}^{2}}+{c}_{2}{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation 

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-3t{y}^{′}+3y=-{t}^{4},\,t>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-3t{y}^{′}+3y=0.
$$

Let $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+3{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+3{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +3] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =1$ and $\lambda =3.$ Thus, the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}{t}^{3}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is proportional to ${t}^{4}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {t}^{4}
$$

where $\alpha $ is the constant that is to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=4\alpha {t}^{3},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=12\alpha {t}^{2}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}(12\alpha {t}^{2})-3t(4\alpha {t}^{3})+3(\alpha {t}^{4}) & =-{t}^{4} \\ (12\alpha -12\alpha +3\alpha ){t}^{4} & =-{t}^{4} \\ 3\alpha {t}^{4} & =-{t}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get $\alpha =-\frac{1}{3}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{{t}^{4}}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2y={t}^{3}{e}^{t},\,t>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)=\frac{A}{t}+B{t}^{2}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ to this equation. 

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:* 

$$
\int {t}^{3}{e}^{t}\text{d}t=({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+6t-6){e}^{t}+C
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the differential equation to the form

$$
{y}^{″}+P(t){y}^{′}+Q(t)y=f(t).
$$

So, we divide both sides of the given equation by ${t}^{2}.$ We get

$$
{y}^{″}-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}y=t{e}^{t}.
$$

We notice that the forcing term $f(t)=t{e}^{t}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions:

$$
{y}_{1}(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,{y}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}
$$

First, let's compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}({t}^{2})^{′}-{(\frac{1}{t})}^{′}{t}^{2} \\  & =2t(\frac{1}{t})-(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}){t}^{2} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(t) & ={y}_{1}(t)u(t)+{y}_{2}(t)v(t),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =-\int \frac{f(t){y}_{2}(t)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}t=-\frac{1}{3}\int {t}^{3}{e}^{t}\text{d}t=-\frac{1}{3}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+6t-6){e}^{t}, \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{f(t){y}_{1}(t)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(t) & ={y}_{1}(t)u(t)+{y}_{2}(t)v(t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3t}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+6t-6){e}^{t}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{3}{e}^{t} \\  & =(-\frac{{t}^{2}}{3}+t-2+\frac{2}{t}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{3}){e}^{t} \\  & =(t-2+\frac{2}{t}){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+4y=4t.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{2t}+Bt{e}^{2t}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ \beta -\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the constants}).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =1$ and $\beta =1,$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t+1.

$$

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}+6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-7y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and sinusoidal forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=\frac{A}{{e}^{7t}}+B{e}^{t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t)+6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡t)-7(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ (-\alpha +6\beta -7\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-\beta -6\alpha -7\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ (-8\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-6\alpha -8\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-8\alpha +6\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ -6\alpha -8\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =-\frac{3}{25}$ and $\beta =-\frac{4}{25},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\frac{4}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\frac{4}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

$$

$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
t^2 y'' - 4ty' + 6y = 2t+6, \quad t > 0
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $2t+6.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
y_p(t) = \alpha t + \beta
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p$ gives

$$
y_p' =  \alpha,
\qquad y_p'' = 0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}(0)-4t(\alpha )+6(\alpha t+\beta ) & =2t+6 \\ (-4\alpha +6\alpha )t+6\beta  & =2t+6 \\ 2\alpha t+6\beta  & =2t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,t) \\ 6\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(t)$ is

$$
y_p(t) = t + 1.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
t^2 y'' +2ty' = t^2 e ^ {t}, \quad t>0
$$

has the complementary solution $y_c(t) =  \dfrac{A}{t} + B,$ find the particular solution $y_p(t)$ to this equation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The right-hand side is not a polynomial, so we need to use another solution technique. Here, we are given the complementary solution $y_c(t) =  \dfrac{A}{t} + B,$ which means that we have two fundamental solutions

$$
y_1(t) = \dfrac{1}{t}  , \qquad y_2(t) = 1.
$$

Because we have two fundamental solutions, we can use variation of parameters.

To use variation of parameters, we must first reduce the differential equation to the form

$$
y'' + P(t) y' +Q(t) y = f(t).
$$

To do this, we divide both sides of the given equation by $t^2,$ and get

$$
y'' + \dfrac{2}{t}y'  =  e ^ {t}.
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
y_1(t) = \dfrac{1}{t}  , \qquad y_2(t) = 1, \qquad f(t) = e^t.
$$

First, let's compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{t})(1)^{′}-{(\frac{1}{t})}^{′}(1) \\  & =0+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  $y_1(t)$ and $y_2(t)$ are independent.

According to the method of variation of parameters, a particular solution of the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(t) & ={y}_{1}(t)u(t)+{y}_{2}(t)v(t),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =-\int \frac{f(t){y}_{2}(t)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}t=-\int {t}^{2}{e}^{t}=-({t}^{2}-2t+2){e}^{t}, \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{f(t){y}_{1}(t)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}t=\int t{e}^{t}=(t-1){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a particular solution is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(t) & ={y}_{1}(t)u(t)+{y}_{2}(t)v(t) \\  & =-\frac{({t}^{2}-2t+2){e}^{t}}{t}+(t-1){e}^{t} \\  & =(1-\frac{2}{t}){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}+y=t.\end{aligned}

,\qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2y_p}{\textrm{d}t^2} = 0.

$$

$$
